Population.evidence_source: This section describes the experiences of participants related to mental illness, sexual minority status, stigma, and isolation, and how these 'offered pathways to suicide'. However, it does not explicitly state the inclusion criteria for recruitment based on a specific suicide experience (e.g., attempted suicide, suicidal ideation, or bereavement).

Area.evidence_source: Participants also experienced an overarching sense of isolation from society as a whole, the underpinnings of which stemmed predominately from having a mental illness and/or being part of a minority sexual group. This was articulated as a lack of belonging and often, as we see below, a sense of moral judgment, in the present, from community, which gave little or no recognition to their biographies, histories, and struggles. This was internalized as stigma, but reflected a problem of feeling like society's burdensome and immoral subjects, from which isolating acts and social practices flowed. The societal and self-stigma endured by most participants highlighted their sense of being a burden and the inherent tensions and stressors at play in openly talking about and/or concealing their embodiment of such immoral subjects. Strongly referenced by participants was societal stigma about mental illness and the isolation actioned by others as illustrated by one participant (age range = 60–69 years): I'm more of a loner . . . being diagnosed with a—mental health disorder, it's not seen by the general public as the same as being diagnosed with any other kind of physical ailment . . . I always find myself feeling separate and feeling the subject of, uh, other people's judgments. Stigmas subordinated this participant and he, like others, spoke about the shunning expereinced in his everyday life. Recursively, the effects of mental illness also fueled many men's excommunication from society. A participant (age range = 40–49 years) linked his mental illness to being without housing and suggested, "It's something I struggle a lot with, when you're in a homeless or down state and people, um, judge you instantly." Stripped of context, this participant argued societal judgments were leveled at men's poor life outcomes, with little consideration or concession to the challenges that had led to those circumstances. The accounts of their mental illness also revealed men's self-stigma, wherein they focussed on their failures and inabilities to meet societal expectations, and perhaps their own gendered ideals. One man (age range = 50–59 years) listed his shortcomings, highlighting the masculine roles that he had failed to fulfill: Expectations I've had on myself in terms of what I consider to be successes in life—a good father, a good husband, a good provider, um, those are probably at the top of the list, and it's my belief I failed at—at all of those three responsibilities. He went on to belabor his failures amid much selfcriticism. Interestingly, the actual context of meeting such challenges and roles was bypassed. Instead, participants tended to judge their poor outcomes in life (rather than the mediating effects of mental illness), amplifying their self-stigma and isolation. For some gay and bisexual participants, stigmas also emerged around being part of a sexual minority group, wherein a lack of societal openness and acceptance intensified men's isolation. One bisexual participant (age range = 40–49 years), who had a wife and boyfriend, felt compelled to conceal and lie about his intimate relationships despite both partners' agreement to their arrangements. He suggested, "It's the shame, the shaming, societal put-downs, and not just man up and bottle it up, but you can't even talk about who you really are." The pressures to cover and conceal mental illness as well as deviations from heterosexual norms weighed heavily on this man—and his partners. Having to fake their fit with traditional normative conventions also troubled some of the gay participants. One gay man (age range = 20–29 years) talked to a lifetime of mental health struggles in being partially out: I really struggled with my sexuality because I was really confused before and I always hid part of myself so that no one would ever know . . . So basically when I was really struggling with my sexuality . . . I was really depressed and I just hid this secret in my mind. No one ever knew that. Multiple stigmas converged, assigning the men as society's burdensome and immoral subjects, a tension that prompted one participant (age range = 60–69 years) to level a critique of societal structures governing norms on all boys and men. Citing the suicide of a 15-year-old boy who left a note including an apology, "I'm sorry world," this participant submitted Figure 6, which he also titled I'm sorry world in posing and addressing the provocative question, "Why did he need to apologize?" I just think that's the saddest thing, that not only someone young kills themselves, but they have to apologize for ever living. But this, seeing the sign, Wrong Way . . . it jumped out at me that there are signs society puts up telling you what to do or not to do and you can't do it . . . There are still the social expectations of men to be successful in our society. It's a capitalist society. I see a lot of depressed middle-aged men around and they've sort of come to realize they've missed the boat and I think families put expectations on young men, at least traditional families. Men's accounts of societal norms and community expectations provided the final overarching layer on our explication of isolation—its meaning and precedents. The dominant account provided here was that the societal perception of mental illness (and the reception of these men in their communities) was embedded in a set of moral understandings about productive/useful/capable male citizens: a test that they often failed, thus producing a sense of being society's burdensome and immoral subjects. This sense of misrecognition and being cast as an illegitimate member of society encouraged withdrawal, perpetuated isolation (along with the other contributing dynamics outlined above), and offered pathways to suicide.
